About the Home Health Aide event

Home Health Aide is a Health Professions event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing · skills.

Ten in-depth lessons following the HOSA Home Health Aide 2026–27 test plan and all eight Round Two skills, built from the official references (Balduzzi and Leahy, Fuzy and Grafe). Includes a vital-signs reporting drill, an intake-and-output calculator, labeled body-system diagrams, skill step-ordering drills and home-care cases. Always follow the scenario, the care plan and the rating sheets you are given.

Home Health Aide lessons

Unit 1 · The aide’s role, communication and safety

Test plan: responsibilities and legal/ethical issues 10%, communication 6%, infection control and safety 10%.

  1. The home health aide: role, responsibilities and law 30 min

    A home health aide works where clients live: their kitchens, bedrooms and bathrooms. That trust brings responsibility. Aides follow a care plan written by a nurse, observe and report changes, protect clients’ rights and…

  2. Communication, observation and reporting 35 min

    The home health aide is the team’s eyes and ears. A nurse might visit once a week, but the aide sees the client several times—and notices the new cough, the untouched lunch or the confusion that was not there yesterday…

  3. Infection control and safety in the home 30 min

    In a hospital, sinks, gloves and sharps containers are everywhere. In a client’s home, the aide brings infection control with them—and also has to notice the loose rug, the overloaded outlet and the oxygen tank next to…

Unit 2 · Basic skills and body systems I

Basic healthcare skills 10% and body systems 40%. Skills I, II and VIII.

  1. Vital signs: tympanic temperature and apical pulse (Skills I–II) 30 min

    Temperature, pulse, respirations and blood pressure are measured at many home visits, and a change can be the first clue to infection, heart problems or dehydration. Two Round Two skills test vital signs directly, and…

  2. Cardiovascular and respiratory care; elasticized stockings (Skill VIII) 30 min

    Many home health clients live with heart failure, high blood pressure or COPD. The aide helps them follow diet and activity plans, use oxygen safely, prevent blood clots with compression stockings and recognize when…

  3. Urinary and digestive care; drainage units and intake and output (Skills III and V) 30 min

    Urine and fluid balance tell a story: dark, scant urine can mean dehydration; cloudy, foul-smelling urine can mean infection; and a client who drinks little and has not voided for eight hours needs a call to the nurse…

Unit 3 · Body systems II

Skin, musculoskeletal, nervous, sensory and endocrine care; nutrition. Skills III–VII.

  1. Skin, bones and mobility; dry dressings and moving up in bed (Skills IV and VII) 35 min

    Two hours in one position can start a pressure injury on a frail client. Dragging a client up in bed can tear fragile skin. The aide’s skills in skin care, positioning and safe movement prevent painful, costly…

  2. Nervous, sensory and endocrine disorders; nutrition and denture care (Skill VI) 30 min

    A stroke can take away speech on one side of the brain and movement on the other side of the body. Diabetes can turn a skipped meal into an emergency. And clean, well-fitting dentures can decide whether an older adult…

Unit 4 · Caring for special populations

Test plan: special populations 24%. Older adults, dementia, mental health, disabilities, newborns, children and end of life.

  1. Older adults, dementia, mental health and disabilities 30 min

    “Dementia” is the general term for a serious loss of mental abilities such as thinking, remembering, reasoning and communicating—and Alzheimer’s disease is its most common cause. Caring for special populations is 24% of…

  2. Mothers, newborns, children and end-of-life care 30 min

    A dying client tells the home health aide, “Please leave me alone; I just want to be by myself.” Recognizing this as part of grief—and responding with respect—is part of caring for clients at the beginning and end of…

Home Health Aide practice tests

Each test is an original, full-length simulation of the HOSA Round One written test, written to run slightly harder than the real thing. Every answer comes with an explanation and a reference.

  • Practice Test 1Full-length Round One simulation50 questions · 60 min
  • Practice Test 2Full-length Round One simulation50 questions · 60 min

Sample Home Health Aide questions

1. To prevent scalds in the home, a water heater should be set no higher than about:

  1. 90 °F
  2. 140 °F
  3. 160 °F
  4. 120 °F
Show answer

D. 120 °F

Setting the water heater at or below 120 °F reduces burn risk, especially for older adults and children with thinner skin or slower reactions.

2. An aide is helping a 6-year-old with a chronic illness. How should procedures be explained?

  1. With detailed medical terms
  2. Only to the parents, never to the child
  3. Not at all, to avoid fear
  4. In simple words suited to the child’s age
Show answer

D. In simple words suited to the child’s age

Using age-appropriate language and honest, simple explanations reduces fear and helps children cooperate.

3. A client begins having a seizure. What should the aide do?

  1. Hold the client down
  2. Put a spoon in the client’s mouth
  3. Protect the head and time the seizure
  4. Give the client water
Show answer

C. Protect the head and time the seizure

Move objects away, cushion the head and never restrain or put anything in the mouth. Time the seizure and call 911 if it lasts more than 5 minutes.
